records.source: Ἦσαν δὲ αὐτῷ ἐγγίζοντες πάντες οἱ τελῶναι καὶ οἱ ἁμαρτωλοὶ ἀκούειν αὐτοῦ.
records.gloss: Were now to him drawing near all the tax collectors and the sinners to hear him.
pieces: Tax collectors and sinners, all of them, kept coming near to listen to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

L.1: Now all the tax collectors and the sinners were coming near to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} to hear {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

R.1: Tax collectors and other people known as sinners kept crowding around Jesus. They all wanted to hear what {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} had to say.

decisions.choice: all: great numbers of them, a way of stressing how many came
alternatives: every single tax collector and sinner in the land
decisions.reason: Luke often uses "all" for a large crowd (5:17; 6:19). The point is that such people kept coming to Jesus.

decisions.choice: tax collectors and sinners: people the religious leaders kept away from
decisions.reason: Tax collectors worked for Rome or its rulers and were known for taking more than was due (3:12-13). "Sinners" were people known for breaking the law or living outside its rules (5:30; 7:37).

decisions.choice: were drawing near: a scene that kept happening, not one visit
decisions.reason: The verb form pictures an ongoing state of affairs. It sets the scene for the three parables that follow.

decisions.choice: other people known as sinners
decisions.reason: Readable shows that "sinners" was a label for a group, as the meaning decision explains.

records.heading: One sheep out of a hundred

records.source: καὶ διεγόγγυζον οἵ τε Φαρισαῖοι καὶ οἱ γραμματεῖς λέγοντες ὅτι Οὗτος ἁμαρτωλοὺς προσδέχεται καὶ συνεσθίει αὐτοῖς.
records.gloss: And were grumbling both the Pharisees and the scribes saying that, This [man] sinners receives and eats with them.
pieces: But the Pharisees and the scribes complained among themselves. "This man welcomes sinners," they said, "and even shares meals with them."

L.2: And both the Pharisees and the scribes were grumbling, saying, "This man receives sinners and eats with them."

R.2: But the Pharisees and the teachers of the law did not like it. They grumbled, "This man makes sinners feel welcome. He even eats with them!"

decisions.choice: were grumbling: the word used of Israel grumbling in the wilderness
decisions.reason: The Greek Old Testament uses this kind of verb for Israel's complaints against Moses and God (Exodus 16:7-8). Luke used it when Jesus ate at Levi's house (5:30) and will use it again at Zacchaeus' house (19:7).

decisions.choice: the Pharisees and the scribes: a Jewish movement devoted to keeping the law in daily life, and the experts who taught the law
decisions.reason: The Pharisees were respected teachers among the people, and many of the scribes belonged to their party (5:30). Both groups were careful about whom they ate with.

decisions.choice: this man: said with scorn
decisions.reason: The leaders do not use Jesus' name. The same kind of phrase is used with scorn in 15:30, "this son of yours".

decisions.choice: receives and eats with: welcomes them as companions at the table
decisions.reason: To share a meal with someone was a sign of friendship and acceptance (5:29-30). The three parables that follow answer this complaint.

decisions.choice: teachers of the law (R); scribes (L, B)
decisions.reason: Readable says what the scribes did, as in 5:30.

decisions.choice: even shares meals with them
decisions.reason: Balanced brings out the force of the complaint, as the meaning decision explains.

records.source: εἶπεν δὲ πρὸς αὐτοὺς τὴν παραβολὴν ταύτην λέγων·
records.gloss: He spoke then to them the parable this saying,
pieces: So Jesus put this parable to them:

L.3: And {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} spoke this parable to them, saying,

R.3: So Jesus told them a story to teach them:

decisions.choice: parable: a story or comparison from everyday life that teaches about God and his kingdom
decisions.reason: As in 8:4 and 12:16. Luke speaks of one parable, though three stories follow: they make one answer to the complaint of 15:2.

decisions.choice: a story to teach them
decisions.reason: Readable says what a parable is, as in 12:16.

decisions.choice: Jesus
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the speaker after the Pharisees' words.

records.source: Τίς ἄνθρωπος ἐξ ὑμῶν ἔχων ἑκατὸν πρόβατα καὶ ἀπολέσας ἐξ αὐτῶν ἓν οὐ καταλείπει τὰ ἐνενήκοντα ἐννέα ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ καὶ πορεύεται ἐπὶ τὸ ἀπολωλὸς ἕως εὕρῃ αὐτό;
records.gloss: What man of you having a hundred sheep and having lost of them one not leaves the ninety nine in the open country and goes after the [one] having been lost until he finds it?
pieces: "Which man among you, if he owned a hundred sheep and lost one of them, would not leave the ninety-nine out in the wild country and search for the lost one until he found it?

L.4: "What man of you, having a hundred sheep and having lost one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the open country and go after the lost one until he finds it?

R.4: "If one of you had a hundred sheep and lost one of them, what would you do? You would leave the other ninety-nine in the open land where they graze. Then you would go and look for the lost sheep until you found it.

decisions.choice: What man of you ... does not: a question that expects the answer that every one of them would
alternatives: a real question about what a shepherd might do
decisions.reason: The question invites the listeners to agree. Any of them would go after a lost animal; so they should understand why Jesus goes after lost people (15:2).

decisions.choice: the open country: wild grazing land, away from towns and fields
decisions.reason: The word means land where no one lives. In Judea it was rough hill country where flocks were taken to graze. The ninety-nine would be left with other shepherds or in a fold; the story does not stop to say.

decisions.choice: goes after the lost one: the shepherd who seeks the lost
decisions.reason: In Ezekiel 34:11-16 God himself promises to search for his scattered sheep and bring back the lost. Jesus says of himself that he came to seek and save the lost (19:10).

decisions.choice: lost: gone missing, strayed away
decisions.reason: The verb can mean destroy or perish (15:17), but with a sheep or a coin it means missing. The same word links all three parables (15:6, 9, 24, 32).

decisions.choice: a question to the listeners, then the answer in two statements, using "you"
alternatives: What man of you ... does not ...?
decisions.reason: Readable breaks up the long question and speaks to the listeners directly, as the Greek "of you" invites. Literal and Balanced keep the question.

decisions.choice: the quotation opens here and runs on to 15:10
decisions.reason: The sheep and the coin are one speech of Jesus. Luke's "He said" in 15:11 starts a new quotation.

records.source: καὶ εὑρὼν ἐπιτίθησιν ἐπὶ τοὺς ὤμους αὐτοῦ χαίρων, καὶ ἐλθὼν εἰς τὸν οἶκον συγκαλεῖ τοὺς φίλους καὶ τοὺς γείτονας, λέγων αὐτοῖς· Συγχάρητέ μοι ὅτι εὗρον τὸ πρόβατόν μου τὸ ἀπολωλός.
records.gloss: And having found [it] he lays [it] on the shoulders of him rejoicing, \v 6 and having come to the house he calls together the friends and the neighbors saying to them, Rejoice with me, for I have found the sheep of me the [one] having been lost.
pieces: And when he finds it, he hoists it onto his shoulders, delighted.
Back at home, he invites his friends and neighbors over. 'Celebrate with me,' he tells them, 'because the sheep I lost has been found.'

L.5: And having found [it], he lays [it] on his shoulders, rejoicing,
L.6: and coming to the house, he calls together the friends and the neighbors, saying to them, 'Rejoice with me, for I have found my sheep that was lost.'

R.5: When you found it, you would be so glad that you would lift it up onto your shoulders and carry it.
R.6: You would go home and get your friends and neighbors together. You would say to them, 'Be glad with me! I have found my lost sheep!'

decisions.choice: lays it on his shoulders: the usual way to carry a sheep, with its legs held at the front
decisions.reason: A tired or frightened sheep may not follow, so the shepherd carries it the whole way home. He does it gladly, not as a burden.

decisions.choice: rejoice with me: share my joy
decisions.reason: The verb means to rejoice together. The finder wants others to share the gladness, as the father does in 15:23-24 and as the elder son refuses to do (15:28).

decisions.choice: that was lost: the sheep that had been lost
decisions.reason: The participle describes the sheep's state before it was found.

decisions.choice: because the sheep I lost has been found
alternatives: for I have found my sheep that was lost
decisions.reason: Balanced puts the lost sheep first, which reads naturally and keeps the meaning.

decisions.choice: you would be so glad
decisions.reason: Readable keeps the "you" of 15:4 and makes the man's gladness its own clause.

records.source: λέγω ὑμῖν ὅτι οὕτως χαρὰ ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ ἔσται ἐπὶ ἑνὶ ἁμαρτωλῷ μετανοοῦντι ἢ ἐπὶ ἐνενήκοντα ἐννέα δικαίοις οἵτινες οὐ χρείαν ἔχουσιν μετανοίας.
records.gloss: I say to you that in the same way joy in the heaven there will be over one sinner repenting rather than over ninety nine righteous ones who no need have of repentance.
pieces: In the same way, I tell you, one sinner who repents will bring more joy in heaven than ninety-nine righteous people who have no need to repent.

L.7: I tell you that in the same way there will be joy in heaven over one sinner who repents, [more] than over ninety-nine righteous [people] who have no need of repentance.

R.7: I tell you, it is the same in heaven. When one sinner turns away from sin and comes back to God, there is joy in heaven. There is more joy over that one person than over ninety-nine people who are already right with God and do not need to turn back.

decisions.choice: in heaven: with God, who lives in heaven
decisions.reason: Jewish speech often said "heaven" in place of God's name, out of reverence (15:18). The joy in heaven is God's own joy.

decisions.choice: rather than: more ... than, a comparison
alternatives: instead of: there is no joy over the ninety-nine
decisions.reason: The word means "than" after a comparison that is left unsaid. The point is the special gladness over the one who comes back, not that God takes no pleasure in the others.

decisions.choice: repents; repentance: turning from sin back to God
decisions.reason: The same words John and Jesus used (3:3; 5:32). In the parable the sheep is found by the shepherd; in the saying the sinner turns back. Both are true of what happens when Jesus welcomes sinners.

decisions.choice: righteous people who have no need of repentance: people who keep the law, or who think they do
alternatives: people who have no sin at all
decisions.reason: Jesus speaks in his hearers' own terms, as in 5:32. Luke tells of some who trusted that they were righteous (18:9). Whether there is irony here is left for the listeners to see.

decisions.choice: [more]
decisions.reason: Literal supplies the comparison the Greek leaves implied.

decisions.choice: turns away from sin and comes back to God; people who are already right with God; do not need to turn back
decisions.reason: Readable explains both words, as in 5:32.

records.source: Ἢ τίς γυνὴ δραχμὰς ἔχουσα δέκα, ἐὰν ἀπολέσῃ δραχμὴν μίαν, οὐχὶ ἅπτει λύχνον καὶ σαροῖ τὴν οἰκίαν καὶ ζητεῖ ἐπιμελῶς ἕως οὗ εὕρῃ;
records.gloss: Or what woman drachmas having ten, if she should lose drachma one, not lights a lamp and sweeps the house and seeks carefully until that she finds [it]?
pieces: Or what woman with ten silver coins, if she lost one of them, would not light a lamp, sweep out her house and hunt for it carefully until she found it?

L.8: Or what woman, having ten drachmas, if she loses one drachma, does not light a lamp and sweep the house and search carefully until she finds [it]?

R.8: Or think about a woman who has ten silver coins. If she loses one of them, she will light a lamp and sweep the whole house. She will look carefully everywhere until she finds it.

decisions.choice: drachma: a Greek silver coin worth about a day's wages
decisions.reason: A drachma was worth about the same as a Roman denarius, the day's wage of a laborer (Matthew 20:2). Ten of them were a large sum for a poor household, perhaps her savings, so the loss of one was serious.

decisions.choice: lights a lamp and sweeps the house: searching a dark house with a dirt or stone floor
decisions.reason: Village houses had small windows and floors of beaten earth or stone. A small coin could be found only with a lamp and a broom.

decisions.choice: Or what woman ... does not: a second question that expects the answer that any woman would
decisions.reason: The second parable has the same shape as the first (15:4). A woman stands beside the shepherd as a picture of God seeking the lost.

decisions.choice: silver coins (B, R); drachmas (L)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the coin's name. Balanced and Readable say what kind of coin it was, as Readable does with the denarius in 10:35; the meaning decision gives its value.

decisions.choice: two statements
decisions.reason: Readable gives the answer to the question, as in 15:4.

records.heading: A coin swept for and found

records.source: καὶ εὑροῦσα συγκαλεῖ τὰς φίλας καὶ γείτονας λέγουσα· Συγχάρητέ μοι ὅτι εὗρον τὴν δραχμὴν ἣν ἀπώλεσα.
records.gloss: And having found [it] she calls together the friends and neighbors saying, Rejoice with me, for I have found the drachma that I lost.
pieces: When she finds it, she gathers her friends and neighbors. 'Be glad with me,' she says, 'for the coin I had lost is found.'

L.9: And having found [it], she calls together the friends and neighbors, saying, 'Rejoice with me, for I have found the drachma that I lost.'

R.9: When she finds it, she asks her friends and neighbors to come over. She says to them, 'Be happy with me! I found the coin I lost!'

decisions.choice: rejoice with me: share my joy
decisions.reason: As in 15:6. The friends here are women, as the Greek forms show.

decisions.choice: that I lost: she owns the loss
decisions.reason: The shepherd speaks of the sheep that was lost; the woman says plainly that she lost the coin. Either way, the owner goes looking.

decisions.choice: coin (B, R); drachma (L)
decisions.reason: As in 15:8.

records.source: οὕτως, λέγω ὑμῖν, γίνεται χαρὰ ἐνώπιον τῶν ἀγγέλων τοῦ θεοῦ ἐπὶ ἑνὶ ἁμαρτωλῷ μετανοοῦντι.
records.gloss: Thus I say to you, there is joy before the angels of the God over one sinner repenting.
pieces: So it is, I tell you: when one sinner repents, there is joy before the angels of God."

L.10: Thus, I tell you, there is joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents."

R.10: I tell you, it is the same with God. When just one sinner turns away from sin and comes back to God, there is joy in the presence of God's angels."

decisions.choice: joy before the angels of God: joy in God's presence, where the angels stand
alternatives: joy felt only by the angels
decisions.reason: "Before" means in the presence of. It is a reverent way of speaking about God's own joy, which his angels see and share (compare 15:7, "in heaven"; 12:8-9).

decisions.choice: repents: turns from sin back to God
decisions.reason: As in 15:7.

decisions.choice: turns away from sin and comes back to God
decisions.reason: Readable explains the word, as in 15:7.

decisions.choice: the quotation closes here
decisions.reason: Luke's own words in 15:11 interrupt Jesus' speech, so the quotation closes and opens again, as at 6:39.

records.source: Εἶπεν δέ· Ἄνθρωπός τις εἶχεν δύο υἱούς.
records.gloss: He said then, A man certain had two sons.
pieces: Then {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said, "A man had two sons.

L.11: And {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said, "A certain man had two sons.

R.11: Then Jesus told another story: "There was once a man who had two sons.

decisions.choice: a man had two sons: the story is about both sons and their father
alternatives: a story about the younger son alone
decisions.reason: The opening words name two sons. The second half of the story (15:25-32) is about the elder son, who answers to the grumbling of 15:2.

decisions.choice: a man: a figure in a parable
decisions.reason: The father's welcome pictures God's welcome of sinners, but he is a character in a story, and the text speaks of him as a man.

decisions.choice: Jesus told another story
decisions.reason: Readable names the speaker and shows that a new story begins.

decisions.choice: the quotation opens here and runs on to 15:32; the speakers' words are in single quotation marks, and words they plan or quote in double ones
alternatives: a new quotation for each speaker
decisions.reason: The story is one speech of Jesus with the speakers' words inside it.

records.heading: A father and his two sons

records.source: καὶ εἶπεν ὁ νεώτερος αὐτῶν τῷ πατρί· Πάτερ, δός μοι τὸ ἐπιβάλλον μέρος τῆς οὐσίας· ὁ δὲ διεῖλεν αὐτοῖς τὸν βίον.
records.gloss: And said the younger of them to the father, Father, give me the falling [to me] portion of the property. And he divided between them the living.
pieces: The younger son said to his father, 'Father, let me have the part of the estate that will come to me.' So the father split what he had between the two of them.

L.12: And the younger of them said to the father, 'Father, give me the portion of the property that falls [to me].' And he divided the living between them.

R.12: The younger son said to his father, 'Father, give me now the part of your property that I will get one day.' So the father divided everything he owned between his two sons.

decisions.choice: give me the portion that falls to me: his share of the inheritance, asked for while his father is still alive
decisions.reason: A father could divide his property while he lived, but a son had no right to demand it. Under the law the elder son received a double share (Deuteronomy 21:17), so the younger son's share would be a third. The request treats the father as if he were already gone.

decisions.choice: the living: the property a family lives on
decisions.reason: The word means life, and also the means of life: the land and goods that support a household (21:4). The father divides it between both sons (15:31).

decisions.choice: property: what a person owns
decisions.reason: A different word from "living" at the end of the verse, with much the same meaning.

decisions.choice: now ... that I will get one day
decisions.reason: Readable shows that he asked for his inheritance early, as the meaning decision explains.

records.source: καὶ μετ’ οὐ πολλὰς ἡμέρας συναγαγὼν πάντα ὁ νεώτερος υἱὸς ἀπεδήμησεν εἰς χώραν μακράν, καὶ ἐκεῖ διεσκόρπισεν τὴν οὐσίαν αὐτοῦ ζῶν ἀσώτως.
records.gloss: And after not many days having gathered together all the younger son went away into a country distant, and there he wasted the property of him living prodigally.
pieces: Only a few days later the younger son packed up everything he owned and traveled to a far country, where he threw his property away on a reckless way of life.

L.13: And not many days later, having gathered everything together, the younger son went away to a distant country, and there he scattered his property, living wastefully.

R.13: Soon after that, the younger son packed up everything he had and went to a country far away. There he wasted all his money. He lived a reckless life.

decisions.choice: having gathered everything together: collected all he had, perhaps by turning it into money
decisions.reason: The verb can be used of turning property into cash. He took everything with him, so that nothing was left behind.

decisions.choice: scattered: wasted, threw away
decisions.reason: The verb means to scatter, as grain is scattered. It is used of the manager who wastes his master's goods (16:1).

decisions.choice: living wastefully: without care or self-control
decisions.reason: The word describes a life with no restraint, spending without thought. The text does not say here how he spent it; the elder brother later claims it was on prostitutes (15:30).

decisions.choice: a distant country: a land of Gentiles, far from his family and his people
decisions.reason: The pigs of 15:15 show that he was among people who did not keep the law of Moses.

decisions.choice: wasted all his money
decisions.reason: Readable uses everyday words for what he did.

records.source: δαπανήσαντος δὲ αὐτοῦ πάντα ἐγένετο λιμὸς ἰσχυρὰ κατὰ τὴν χώραν ἐκείνην, καὶ αὐτὸς ἤρξατο ὑστερεῖσθαι.
records.gloss: Having spent however of him all, there arose a famine severe throughout the country that, and he began to be in need.
pieces: When he had used up everything, a terrible famine struck that whole land, and he began to go without.

L.14: And when he had spent everything, a severe famine came over that country, and he began to be in need.

R.14: When all his money was gone, a bad famine came to that country. There was very little food, and he did not have what he needed.

decisions.choice: a severe famine: a great shortage of food across the land
alternatives: a time of high prices only
decisions.reason: Famines came when the rains failed or crops were ruined (Genesis 41:54-57; Acts 11:28). The story makes his ruin complete: his money is gone just when food is scarce.

decisions.choice: to be in need: to lack what he needed to live
decisions.reason: The verb means to fall short or lack. It is the start of real hunger (15:17).

decisions.choice: There was very little food
decisions.reason: Readable explains the word "famine".

records.source: καὶ πορευθεὶς ἐκολλήθη ἑνὶ τῶν πολιτῶν τῆς χώρας ἐκείνης, καὶ ἔπεμψεν αὐτὸν εἰς τοὺς ἀγροὺς αὐτοῦ βόσκειν χοίρους·
records.gloss: And having gone he joined himself to one of the citizens of the country that, and he sent him into the fields of him to feed pigs.
pieces: So he went and attached himself to one of the people of that country, and the man sent him out into his fields to look after pigs.

L.15: And going, he attached himself to one of the citizens of that country, and he sent him into his fields to feed pigs.

R.15: So he went to work for a man who lived in that country. The man sent him into his fields to feed his pigs.

decisions.choice: attached himself to: went to him and would not let go, as one who begs for work
decisions.reason: The verb means to be glued or joined to. He pressed himself on a stranger to get any work at all.

decisions.choice: to feed pigs: the lowest work a Jewish man could imagine
decisions.reason: The law of Moses called pigs unclean (Leviticus 11:7; Deuteronomy 14:8). A Jew who fed pigs for a Gentile had fallen as low as he could.

decisions.choice: the man
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable make clear who sent whom.

records.source: καὶ ἐπεθύμει γεμίσαι τὴν κοιλίαν αὐτοῦ ἀπὸ τῶν κερατίων ὧν ἤσθιον οἱ χοῖροι, καὶ οὐδεὶς ἐδίδου αὐτῷ.
records.gloss: And he was longing to fill the belly of him from the pods that were eating the pigs, and no one was giving to him.
pieces: He wished he could fill himself up with the carob pods the pigs were eating, but no one gave him a thing.

L.16: And he was longing to fill his belly from the pods that the pigs were eating, and no one was giving [anything] to him.

R.16: He was so hungry that he wanted to eat the bean pods that the pigs were eating. But no one gave him any food.

decisions.choice: pods: the pods of the carob tree, used to feed animals
decisions.reason: Carob pods are long, sweet and tough. They were fed to animals, and only the very poor ate them.

decisions.choice: to fill his belly (SBLGNT)
alternatives: to be fed, to be satisfied
decisions.reason: Many manuscripts read "to fill his belly". Some early ones, among them Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, read "to be satisfied" from the pods. The meaning is much the same: he was starving. Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: no one was giving to him: no one gave him food, not even the pods
decisions.reason: The verb has no object. Its point is that no one cared for him at all.

decisions.choice: [anything]
decisions.reason: Literal supplies the object English needs.

decisions.choice: carob pods (B); bean pods (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced names the plant; Readable describes it.

records.source: εἰς ἑαυτὸν δὲ ἐλθὼν ἔφη· Πόσοι μίσθιοι τοῦ πατρός μου περισσεύονται ἄρτων, ἐγὼ δὲ λιμῷ ὧδε ἀπόλλυμαι·
records.gloss: To himself however having come he was saying, How many hired servants of the father of me have abundance of bread, I however with hunger here am perishing!
pieces: At last he saw his situation clearly. 'So many of my father's hired workers have more bread than they can eat,' he said, 'while I am dying of hunger here!

L.17: But coming to himself, he said, 'How many of my father's hired workers have more than enough bread, but I am perishing here with hunger!

R.17: Then he began to think clearly. He said to himself, 'My father has many hired workers, and they all have more food than they need. But here I am, about to die because I have nothing to eat!

decisions.choice: coming to himself: coming to his senses, seeing clearly
decisions.reason: The phrase was used of someone who returns to a right mind. It is the turning point of his story; what follows shows what it led to.

decisions.choice: hired workers: day laborers paid wages, not slaves of the household
decisions.reason: The word is different from the word for slaves in 15:22. Hired workers were paid by the day and had no place in the family (Matthew 20:1-2). Even they ate well at his father's house.

decisions.choice: perishing: dying
decisions.reason: The verb is the one used for the lost sheep and coin (15:4, 9). Here it has its plain meaning: he is starving.

decisions.choice: how many: an exclamation, not a question
alternatives: a question asking for a number
decisions.reason: He is not counting; he is amazed at the plenty in his father's house.

decisions.choice: he saw his situation clearly (B); he began to think clearly (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the meaning of the idiom, which Literal keeps.

decisions.choice: his words open here and run on to 15:19
decisions.reason: The Greek goes straight on from what he says to what he will do and say.

records.source: ἀναστὰς πορεύσομαι πρὸς τὸν πατέρα μου καὶ ἐρῶ αὐτῷ· Πάτερ, ἥμαρτον εἰς τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ ἐνώπιόν σου, οὐκέτι εἰμὶ ἄξιος κληθῆναι υἱός σου· ποίησόν με ὡς ἕνα τῶν μισθίων σου.
records.gloss: Having risen up I will go to the father of me and I will say to him, Father, I have sinned against the heaven and before you; \v 19 no longer am I worthy to be called son of you; make me like one of the hired servants of you.
pieces: I will get up and go back to my father, and I will tell him, "Father, I have sinned against heaven and in your sight.
I do not deserve to be called your son any longer. Take me on as one of your hired workers."'

L.18: Getting up, I will go to my father and will say to him, "Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you;
L.19: I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Make me like one of your hired workers."'

R.18: I will leave this place and go back to my father. I will say to him, "Father, I have sinned against God and against you.
R.19: I am not good enough to be called your son anymore. Please let me be one of the workers you pay."'

decisions.choice: against heaven: against God
decisions.reason: Out of reverence, Jewish speech often said "heaven" in place of God's name (15:7; Daniel 4:26). He has wronged God and his father both.

decisions.choice: I have sinned against ... and before you: the language of confession in Scripture
decisions.reason: Pharaoh used similar words to Moses (Exodus 10:16), and David confessed his sin against the Lord (2 Samuel 12:13; Psalm 51:6).

decisions.choice: worthy to be called your son: fit to be treated as a son
decisions.reason: He knows he has thrown away the place of a son. He hopes only for the place of a hired worker.

decisions.choice: hired workers: day laborers paid wages
decisions.reason: As in 15:17.

decisions.choice: against God
decisions.reason: Readable names God, as the meaning decision explains.

decisions.choice: his words close here; the words he plans to say are in double quotation marks
decisions.reason: The words he will say to his father are a quotation inside his own words.

records.source: καὶ ἀναστὰς ἦλθεν πρὸς τὸν πατέρα ἑαυτοῦ.
records.gloss: And having risen up he went to the father of himself.
pieces: So he set off and went back to his father.

L.20: And getting up, he went to his own father.

R.20: So he got up and started back home to his father.

decisions.choice: having risen up, he went: he did what he had said he would do (15:18)
alternatives: he stood up from where he sat
decisions.reason: The same words as his plan in 15:18. "Rising up" here means setting out.

decisions.choice: set off (B); got up and started back home (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the sense of starting out.

records.source: ἔτι δὲ αὐτοῦ μακρὰν ἀπέχοντος εἶδεν αὐτὸν ὁ πατὴρ αὐτοῦ καὶ ἐσπλαγχνίσθη καὶ δραμὼν ἐπέπεσεν ἐπὶ τὸν τράχηλον αὐτοῦ καὶ κατεφίλησεν αὐτόν.
records.gloss: Still now he far being distant saw him the father of him and was moved with compassion, and having run he fell upon the neck of him and kissed him.
pieces: His father caught sight of him while he was still far away, and his heart went out to him. He ran to meet him, embraced him and kissed him warmly.

L.20: But while he was still far off, his father saw him and was moved with compassion, and running, he fell upon his neck and kissed him.

R.20: While the son was still far down the road, his father saw him coming. He felt great love and pity for his son. He ran to him, hugged him, and kissed him again and again.

decisions.choice: was moved with compassion: was stirred to the depths by love and pity
alternatives: felt sorry in a distant way
decisions.reason: The verb comes from the word for a person's inward parts, where deep feelings were felt. Luke uses it of Jesus at Nain (7:13) and of the Samaritan (10:33).

decisions.choice: while he was still far off, his father saw him: the father was watching for him
decisions.reason: The father sees him first and runs to him before the son can say a word. The text does not say he had been watching, but the story suggests it.

decisions.choice: fell upon his neck: threw his arms around him
decisions.reason: The phrase is used of a warm embrace, as when Esau met Jacob (Genesis 33:4) and Joseph met his father (Genesis 46:29).

decisions.choice: kissed: kissed warmly, again and again
decisions.reason: The verb is a stronger form of the usual word for a kiss (7:38, 45).

decisions.choice: having run: an older man running to meet his son
decisions.reason: A head of a household did not usually run. The father puts dignity aside to reach his son.

decisions.choice: his heart went out to him
decisions.reason: Balanced uses an everyday phrase for the deep feeling, as in 10:33.

records.source: εἶπεν δὲ ὁ υἱὸς αὐτῷ· Πάτερ, ἥμαρτον εἰς τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ ἐνώπιόν σου, οὐκέτι εἰμὶ ἄξιος κληθῆναι υἱός σου.
records.gloss: Said then the son to him, Father, I have sinned against the heaven and before you, no longer am I worthy to be called son of you.
pieces: His son said to him, 'Father, I have sinned against heaven and in your sight. I do not deserve to be called your son any longer.'

L.21: And the son said to him, 'Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; I am no longer worthy to be called your son.'

R.21: The son said, 'Father, I have sinned against God and against you. I am not good enough to be called your son anymore.'

decisions.choice: the son's words end with "your son" (SBLGNT)
alternatives: the son's words go on: "make me like one of your hired workers"
decisions.reason: Some early manuscripts, among them Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, add the last line of the speech he planned (15:19). Most manuscripts do not have it, and it may have been added to match 15:19. Without it, the father breaks in before the son can ask to be a hired worker. Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: against heaven: against God
decisions.reason: As in 15:18.

decisions.choice: against God
decisions.reason: As in 15:18.

records.source: εἶπεν δὲ ὁ πατὴρ πρὸς τοὺς δούλους αὐτοῦ· Ταχὺ ἐξενέγκατε στολὴν τὴν πρώτην καὶ ἐνδύσατε αὐτόν, καὶ δότε δακτύλιον εἰς τὴν χεῖρα αὐτοῦ καὶ ὑποδήματα εἰς τοὺς πόδας, καὶ φέρετε τὸν μόσχον τὸν σιτευτόν, θύσατε, καὶ φαγόντες εὐφρανθῶμεν, ὅτι οὗτος ὁ υἱός μου νεκρὸς ἦν καὶ ἀνέζησεν, ἦν ἀπολωλὼς καὶ εὑρέθη.
records.gloss: Said then the father to the slaves of him, Quickly bring out a robe the best and clothe him, and give a ring for the hand of him and sandals for the feet, \v 23 and bring the calf the fattened, kill [it], and having eaten let us be merry, \v 24 for this the son of me dead was and is alive again, he was lost and is found.
pieces: But the father said to his servants, 'Hurry! Bring out the finest robe and dress him in it. Give him a ring for his hand and sandals for his feet.
Fetch the calf we have been fattening and slaughter it. Let us eat and celebrate,
for my son here was dead, and now he lives again. He was lost, and now he has been found.'

L.22: But the father said to his slaves, 'Quickly, bring out a robe, the best [one], and clothe him, and give [him] a ring for his hand and sandals for [his] feet,
L.23: and bring the fattened calf, kill [it], and let us eat and celebrate,
L.24: because this son of mine was dead and has come to life again; he was lost and has been found.'

R.22: But the father called to his servants, 'Be quick! Go and get the best robe we have and put it on my son. Give him a ring to wear on his hand, and sandals for his feet.
R.23: Bring the calf that we have been feeding to make it fat, and kill it. We will have a big meal and a party!
R.24: My son here was dead, but he is alive again. He was lost, but now he is found.'

decisions.choice: slaves: members of the household who belonged to the father
decisions.reason: The word is the usual word for a slave, different from the hired workers of 15:17 and 19. The father has slaves at his command; the son had hoped only to be a hired worker.

decisions.choice: the best robe, a ring, sandals: signs that he is welcomed as a son with honor
alternatives: simple clothing for a poor man
decisions.reason: A fine robe was given to honor a person (Genesis 41:42; Esther 6:7-11). A ring could carry a family seal and showed standing in the household (Genesis 41:42). Slaves and hired workers often went barefoot; sandals marked a free son.

decisions.choice: the fattened calf: a calf kept and fed for a special feast
decisions.reason: Meat was rarely eaten in ordinary homes. A calf fattened on grain was kept for a great occasion and would feed a whole village (Genesis 18:7; 1 Samuel 28:24).

decisions.choice: was dead and has come to life; was lost and has been found: he was cut off from his father, and now he is restored
decisions.reason: The son had not died, but he was as good as dead to his family. The pairs pick up the lost sheep and coin (15:6, 9) and speak of the new life that comes when a sinner returns (15:7, 10).

decisions.choice: let us celebrate: let us feast and be glad together
decisions.reason: The verb means to be glad and merry, and is used of feasting (12:19; 16:19). The same verb is used in 15:24, 29 and 32.

decisions.choice: dress him in it (B); put it on my son (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use everyday wording for putting on the robe. The father tells the servants to "give" the ring and sandals, and all three levels keep that verb.

decisions.choice: We will have a big meal and a party!
alternatives: having eaten, let us be merry
decisions.reason: Readable uses everyday words for a feast and a celebration.

decisions.choice: servants
decisions.reason: "Servant" in Balanced and Readable, as the style guide has it; the meaning decision (m1) keeps that the person was owned, and Literal keeps "slave".

records.source: καὶ ἤρξαντο εὐφραίνεσθαι.
records.gloss: And they began to be merry.
pieces: And the celebration began.

decisions.choice: they began to be merry: the feast is under way when the elder son comes home
decisions.reason: "Began" leads into the next scene: the music and dancing are still going on in 15:25.

decisions.choice: the celebration began
decisions.reason: Balanced makes the celebration the subject; the meaning is the same.

records.source: Ἦν δὲ ὁ υἱὸς αὐτοῦ ὁ πρεσβύτερος ἐν ἀγρῷ· καὶ ὡς ἐρχόμενος ἤγγισεν τῇ οἰκίᾳ, ἤκουσεν συμφωνίας καὶ χορῶν, καὶ προσκαλεσάμενος ἕνα τῶν παίδων ἐπυνθάνετο τί ἂν εἴη ταῦτα·
records.gloss: Was now the son of him the elder in [the] field, and while coming he drew near to the house, he heard music and dancing, \v 26 and having called near one of the servants he was asking what might be these things.
pieces: All this time the older son had been out in the field. On his way back, as he came close to the house, the sound of music and dancing reached him.
He called over one of the servants and asked him what this could mean.

L.25: Now his elder son was in the field, and as he came and drew near to the house, he heard music and dancing,
L.26: and calling one of the servants to [him], he asked what these things might be.

R.25: The older son had been working out in the field. As he walked back toward the house, he could hear music and people dancing.
R.26: He called to one of the servants and asked what was happening.

decisions.choice: his elder son was in the field: at work while the feast began
decisions.reason: The elder son is doing his daily work on the farm. He has stayed with his father the whole time (15:29, 31).

decisions.choice: music and dancing: the sounds of a feast
decisions.reason: The first word means music played or sung together; the second, dancing in a group, as at weddings and festivals.

decisions.choice: servants: young household servants or helpers
decisions.reason: The word can mean a child or a servant. Here it is one of the household staff. It is a different word from the slaves of 15:22 and the hired workers of 15:17.

decisions.choice: had been working out in the field
decisions.reason: Readable says why he was in the field, as the meaning decision explains.

records.heading: The older son

records.source: ὁ δὲ εἶπεν αὐτῷ ὅτι Ὁ ἀδελφός σου ἥκει, καὶ ἔθυσεν ὁ πατήρ σου τὸν μόσχον τὸν σιτευτόν, ὅτι ὑγιαίνοντα αὐτὸν ἀπέλαβεν.
records.gloss: He and said to him that, The brother of you is come, and has killed the father of you the calf the fattened, because in good health him he has received back.
pieces: 'Your brother is home,' the servant told him, 'and your father has slaughtered the fattened calf, because his son has come back to him alive and well.'

L.27: And he said to him, 'Your brother has come, and your father has killed the fattened calf, because he has received him back healthy.'

R.27: The servant told him, 'Your brother has come home. Your father killed the calf that was being fattened for a feast, because your brother has come back to him safe and healthy.'

decisions.choice: in good health: safe and well
decisions.reason: The servant reports only the outward facts: the son is alive and well. The father sees more: his son was dead and lives (15:24).

decisions.choice: has received him back: has him back again
alternatives: has taken him in as a guest
decisions.reason: The verb means to get back what was one's own.

decisions.choice: the servant (B, R); his son (B)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the speaker, and Balanced names the one who came back, so that the pronouns stay clear.

records.source: ὠργίσθη δὲ καὶ οὐκ ἤθελεν εἰσελθεῖν.
records.gloss: He was angry however and not was willing to go in.
pieces: At this he grew angry and would not go inside.

L.28: But he became angry and was not willing to go in.

R.28: The older son was angry. He would not go into the house.

decisions.choice: was not willing to go in: he kept refusing
decisions.reason: The verb form shows a stubborn refusal. He shuts himself out of the feast, just as the grumblers of 15:2 will not share Jesus' table with sinners.

decisions.choice: The older son
decisions.reason: Readable names him.

records.source: ὁ δὲ πατὴρ αὐτοῦ ἐξελθὼν παρεκάλει αὐτόν.
records.gloss: The and father of him having gone out was begging him.
pieces: His father came out and appealed to him.

L.28: And his father, coming out, was pleading with him.

R.28: So his father came out and begged him to come in.

decisions.choice: was pleading with: kept urging him, with warmth
decisions.reason: The verb can mean urge, appeal or comfort. Here the father goes out to his elder son, as he ran out to the younger, and appeals to him to come in.

decisions.choice: to come in
decisions.reason: Readable says what the father pleaded for.

records.source: ὁ δὲ ἀποκριθεὶς εἶπεν τῷ πατρὶ αὐτοῦ· Ἰδοὺ τοσαῦτα ἔτη δουλεύω σοι καὶ οὐδέποτε ἐντολήν σου παρῆλθον, καὶ ἐμοὶ οὐδέποτε ἔδωκας ἔριφον ἵνα μετὰ τῶν φίλων μου εὐφρανθῶ·
records.gloss: He and answering said to the father of him, Behold, so many years I serve you and never a commandment of you I disobeyed, and to me never did you give a young goat that with the friends of me I might make merry.
pieces: He replied to his father, 'Listen! For all these years I have worked like a slave for you. Not once have I gone against your orders. And not once have you given me a young goat for a feast with my friends.

L.29: But answering, he said to his father, 'Look, so many years I have been serving you as a slave, and I never disobeyed a command of yours, and you never gave me a young goat so that I might celebrate with my friends.

R.29: But he said to his father, 'Look at all the years I have worked hard for you, like a slave! I have always done what you told me to do. But you never once gave me a young goat, so that I could have a party with my friends.

decisions.choice: I have been serving you: working as a slave works
decisions.reason: The verb is formed from the word for a slave. He sees himself as a slave in his father's house, not as a son, though the father says all he has is his (15:31).

decisions.choice: a young goat: a small animal, worth much less than a fattened calf
decisions.reason: He compares the little he thinks he was given with the great feast for his brother.

decisions.choice: look: an outburst, calling attention to his complaint
alternatives: a word asking him to see something
decisions.reason: He does not greet his father with "Father", as the younger son did (15:21); he begins with a protest.

decisions.choice: Look (L); Listen! (B); Look at (R)
decisions.reason: "Behold" is old-fashioned. Here the word is an angry cry, so Balanced and Readable keep it as an outburst.

decisions.choice: serving you as a slave (L); worked like a slave (B, R)
decisions.reason: The words keep the link with the word for a slave, as the meaning decision explains. "Like a slave" stays at every level, as the style guide keeps "slave" where slavery itself is the point: the elder son sets himself as a slave against the son he is (15:31; meaning decision m1).

decisions.choice: his words open here and run on to 15:30
decisions.reason: The elder son's complaint is one speech.

records.source: ὅτε δὲ ὁ υἱός σου οὗτος ὁ καταφαγών σου τὸν βίον μετὰ πορνῶν ἦλθεν, ἔθυσας αὐτῷ τὸν σιτευτὸν μόσχον.
records.gloss: When however the son of you this, the [one] having devoured of you the living with prostitutes, came, you have killed for him the fattened calf.
pieces: But this son of yours has eaten up your property with prostitutes, and the moment he turns up, you slaughter the fattened calf for him!'

L.30: But when this son of yours came, who devoured your living with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him!'

R.30: But now this son of yours comes home. He wasted your money on prostitutes. And you killed the fat calf for him!'

decisions.choice: this son of yours: said with scorn
decisions.reason: He will not call him "my brother". The father answers with "this brother of yours" (15:32).

decisions.choice: devoured your living: used up the family's property like a glutton
decisions.reason: To devour property is to waste it greedily. The "living" is the father's property (15:12), and he speaks of it as the father's, not his brother's share.

decisions.choice: with prostitutes: the elder son's charge
alternatives: a fact the story has already told
decisions.reason: The story said only that the younger son lived wastefully (15:13). This is the elder son's account of it.

decisions.choice: two statements, then the complaint
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable break up the sentence and keep its angry tone.

decisions.choice: his words close here
decisions.reason: The elder son's speech ends.

records.source: ὁ δὲ εἶπεν αὐτῷ· Τέκνον, σὺ πάντοτε μετ’ ἐμοῦ εἶ, καὶ πάντα τὰ ἐμὰ σά ἐστιν·
records.gloss: He and said to him, Child, you always with me are, and all that [is] mine yours is.
pieces: His father answered, 'My child, you are with me always, and all that is mine belongs to you.

L.31: And he said to him, 'Child, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours.

R.31: The father said, 'My dear son, you have been with me the whole time. All I own is yours.

decisions.choice: child: a tender way to address a son
alternatives: a rebuke, as to a small child
decisions.reason: The word means child. The father speaks gently, even after his son's angry words.

decisions.choice: all that is mine is yours: the rest of the property belongs to him already
decisions.reason: The father divided his property between both sons (15:12). The elder son has lost nothing by his brother's return.

decisions.choice: My dear son
decisions.reason: Readable gives the warmth of the word as a father would say it.

decisions.choice: his words open here and run on to 15:32
decisions.reason: The father's answer is one speech.

records.source: εὐφρανθῆναι δὲ καὶ χαρῆναι ἔδει, ὅτι ὁ ἀδελφός σου οὗτος νεκρὸς ἦν καὶ ἔζησεν, καὶ ἀπολωλὼς καὶ εὑρέθη.
records.gloss: To make merry however and to rejoice it was fitting, because the brother of you this dead was and is alive, and was lost and is found.
pieces: But it was only right to celebrate and rejoice, for this brother of yours was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found.'"

L.32: But it was necessary to celebrate and rejoice, because this brother of yours was dead and has come to life, and [was] lost and has been found.'"

R.32: It was right for us to have a party and be glad. Your brother was dead, and now he lives again! He was lost, and now he has been found!'"

decisions.choice: it was necessary: it was the only right thing to do
decisions.reason: The word means "it must be". It is the word Luke uses for what God's purpose requires (2:49; 9:22). The father could not do otherwise.

decisions.choice: this brother of yours: the father's reply to "this son of yours" (15:30)
alternatives: a plain way of naming him
decisions.reason: The father reminds the elder son that the one who came home is his brother.

decisions.choice: was dead and has come to life; was lost and has been found
decisions.reason: As in 15:24.

decisions.choice: the story ends without saying whether the elder son went in
alternatives: the elder son refused for good
decisions.reason: Jesus leaves the ending open. The listeners who grumbled in 15:2 must decide for themselves whether they will join the feast.

decisions.choice: the father's words and Jesus' speech close here
decisions.reason: The parable that began in 15:11 ends with the chapter.
